title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Operating Cycles
web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Operating Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business Got Here — Past Cycles & Pivots
question: How did a Mumbai trading concern become a ₹2,700 Cr technology distributor and brand owner, and what do its past cycles say about how reliably it turns growth into cash?

epigraph.quote: Cash is a fact; profit is an opinion.
epigraph.author: Accounting maxim, commonly attributed to Alfred Rappaport

web_blocks.text: Creative Newtech's history is three stories told at once. One is a founder who kept adding vendors to a Mumbai trading house. Another is a trademark licence that created a second and richer business offshore. The third is a balance sheet that has repeatedly been asked to fund growth faster than operations could pay for it. Between FY19 and FY26 consolidated total income grew from ₹370.70 Cr to ₹2,717.51 Cr, a 33% compound rate [2]. PAT grew from ₹5.85 Cr to ₹70.29 Cr [2]. Over the same eight years the cash-flow statement shows cumulative operating cash flow of about −₹328 Cr against cumulative reported PAT of ₹241 Cr [12]. Those two facts are the spine of this chapter. Growth has been real. Converting growth into cash has been the exception. Management's multi-year promises have been more reliable on revenue than on cash, margin or the size of the licence business.

web_blocks.title: Origin: a one-man trading concern that became a principal-to-principal distributor

web_blocks.text: Ketan Patel started a proprietary concern, Creative Computers, in 1992 as a pure trading business with ten employees. A later investor-deck timeline says two, so treat the headcount as folklore and the year as fact [9]. The company was incorporated on 22 September 2004 and took over the proprietorship in 2005. It became a public limited company in March 2017, just before its IPO [9]. The first lines were Microsoft hardware, Epson printers and AOC monitors. The company's own timeline adds Epson dot-matrix printer aggregation and Microsoft sub-distribution in Maharashtra and Gujarat, then branches in Pune, Bangalore and Ahmedabad (Q4 FY23 investor presentation). By FY16 the business booked ₹198.79 Cr of sales through about 20 branches and roughly 6,000 dealers. It bought in bulk from vendors on its own account and sold to resellers, sub-distributors, system integrators and retailers [9]. That principal-to-principal model is the root of every number that follows. The margin is the thin spread between the vendor's price and the reseller's price, so profit depends on how fast inventory leaves and receivables come back.

The step that changed the economics came in 2015–16. Creative signed a trademark licence with Honeywell International dated 4 December 2015, then valid to 31 December 2020, with royalty payable on net sales [9]. The annual report dates the programme from September 2016 [1]. The licence does not make Creative a distributor of Honeywell goods. Creative designs the products, selects contract factories (about 28 facilities across Asia today) and sells Honeywell-branded electronics. It pays Honeywell a minimum guarantee or a percentage of sales, whichever is higher [1] (Q1 FY24 call). Honeywell audits the factories, approves every pack through its design-language system and scores the licensee each quarter on 10 to 12 parameters. Ketan Patel reported a 4.8 out of 5 in the latest quarterly review before the May 2025 call [6]. The licence sits in Secure Connection Limited, a Hong Kong company incorporated on 21 February 2017 [1]. By FY26 the Brand segment generated ₹380.86 Cr of consolidated revenue [1]. How far that business can scale, and on what renewal terms, is the most important structural question in the company's history.

web_blocks.text: Read the table for the pattern behind the dates. Each pivot answered the thin spread. Imaging and lifestyle brands paid more than IT peripherals. Honeywell paid far more than either, and sat offshore. CKart was meant to cut the cost to serve dealers. Enterprise trade absorbed fixed cost in years when cash was spare. Make-in-India vendors and owned brands are the latest answer. Management says the distribution book still earns its place because it will 'amortize our cost completely', give 'a foot in the door' and supply market intelligence [7]. The consistent feature is that none of these moves shrank the working capital a distributor must carry, which is why the cash story below repeats.

web_blocks.title: How the Honeywell structure shapes group economics

web_blocks.text: Housing the licence offshore has three consequences. First, tax: consolidated tax was ₹11.47 Cr in FY26, exactly the parent's own charge, on consolidated pre-tax profit of ₹81.76 Cr against ₹45.82 Cr standalone. The subsidiary's profit therefore bore no tax, and the effective consolidated rate was about 14% [3]. The CFO explained the mechanism in October 2024: Hong Kong levies no tax on export sales (Q2 FY25 call). Second, minority leakage: Creative owns 77.50% of Secure Connection and its chief executive Mohit Anand owns the rest, so ₹8.42 Cr of FY26 consolidated PAT (12.0%) belonged to non-controlling interest [1][8]. Third, related-party flow: the Indian parent bought ₹155.39 Cr of goods from Secure Connection in FY26 (₹100.09 Cr in FY25) [1]. Shareholders were asked to approve up to ₹750 Cr of such transactions for FY27 [1]. The structure is efficient and transparent in the filings. It also means a large part of group profit sits in an entity that is neither fully owned nor taxed.

Creative's stake in Secure Connection rose from 52.5% to 77.5% through two share swaps. In August 2023 it issued 5,80,000 shares at ₹450 (₹26.10 Cr) to Sapri Trading DWC LLC for 2,267 Secure Connection shares, lifting the stake to 69.5% (release). In March 2024 it issued 57,325 shares at ₹785 (₹4.50 Cr) to V. D. Patel for 1,066 shares (AR FY24). The CFO's rationale was that a minority holder in an unlisted company has no exit while the whole profitable Honeywell business sat in that subsidiary [8]. The CKart B2B platform went the other way: a slump sale to World Goods Marketplace Pvt Ltd for ₹10 Cr in March 2024. It booked a ₹9.9 Cr gain in other income [8] (AR FY24). The buyer appears in the FY26 related-party schedule [1]. The CyberPowerPC joint venture is held through Creative Ecommerce Ventures (Q3 FY25 deck), in which Creative holds 49%. That followed the purchase of 8,51,700 shares for ₹4.26 Cr by two outside investors in FY25, which made it an associate rather than a subsidiary [1]. Rinavaa Technologies, sometimes listed among group entities, is not a subsidiary. It is a related party on whose board the chairman and a whole-time director sit, with a ₹91.5 lakh advance payable [1].

The structure is still growing. Two step-down subsidiaries of Secure Connection (a US LLC and a Shenzhen technology company) were incorporated in H1 FY27 with no significant operations [10]. A Singapore procurement subsidiary with initial capital of up to USD 10,000 was approved on 4 November 2026 (board outcome). Two acquisitions are pending. The first is Infinova (India) Pvt Ltd, with a board budget of up to USD 4.00 Million (release). Management expected it to close by mid-November plus about 15 days for foreign-exchange approvals [4]. The second is Zicom SaaS Pvt Ltd, at an enterprise value of ₹50.50 Cr, of which ₹25.00 Cr is cash and ₹25.50 Cr is shares. It is subject to an extraordinary general meeting on 28 November 2026 (release). Neither contributes to reported revenue yet.

web_blocks.takeaway: Every round was priced above the last (₹75, ₹110, ₹450, ₹785, ₹1,133.33). The cash raised after the IPO is small next to the cash the operations have absorbed. [9][8]

web_blocks.text: The dilution arithmetic is gentler than the cash arithmetic. Shares outstanding went from 1,16,00,000 at the start of FY22 to 1,50,16,675 from January 2025. That is an increase of 34,16,675 shares or 29.5% (AR FY23) [1]. Of that, 10,00,000 shares came from the 2021 issue, 17,79,350 from the 2023 shares and warrants, and 6,37,325 from the two swaps. Reported earnings per share still rose roughly threefold, from ₹13.32 in FY22 [12] to ₹41.04 in FY26 [1], because profit grew faster than the share count. The pending ESOP pool and the Zicom swap would add 4,25,000 shares, another 2.8% of today's capital. Promoter holding was 56.62% at March 2026, down from 56.91% in December 2023 [12]; Ketan Patel personally holds 84,39,520 shares, 56.2% of the total [1].

Set that against cash. Cash equity raised after the IPO totals about ₹91 Cr (₹11.00 Cr in 2021, ₹39.10 Cr of shares and ₹40.97 Cr of warrants in 2023). Over FY22 to FY26 cumulative operating cash flow was about −₹318 Cr [12]. Equity funded under 30% of the operating outflow. The rest came from borrowings, which rose from ₹64 Cr at March 2022 to ₹324 Cr at March 2026 [12], and from supplier credit. Management says no equity raise is planned for working capital over the next 15 months. A raise would follow only an acquisition of roughly 30% of the company's size [5]. The Zicom share swap shows a different instinct: paying for acquisitions partly in paper.

Two changes matter. Chief financial officer: Abhijit Kanvinde presented the financials on every call in the data set from May 2022 to November 2025. He resigned on 14 April 2026. Ajit Thakur, hired as Vice President–Finance on 4 December 2025, became CFO on 14 May 2026, the day before the FY26 results call [1] (CFO appointment). That reads as a planned handover rather than a walkout, since the successor was in the building for four and a half months. The timing is still awkward, because the resignation came a month before audited results that showed receivables up 138% and operating cash flow of −₹271.88 Cr [1]. The filings do not say why he left. The new CFO's first guidance was candid: he called the 45-day working-capital level reached in September 2026 unsustainable and pointed to 52 to 55 days [4].

Second, the board. Purvi Patel, co-founder and wife of the chairman, resigned as whole-time director on 11 August 2025 'to pursue philanthropic and social work independently'. She was re-engaged on 26 August 2025 as President–Strategy and Sustainability, later styled Chief Strategy Officer. The role carries unchanged pay of ₹81.68 lakh for FY26 and ₹115.10 lakh proposed for FY27, an office of profit that shareholders approved (AR FY25) [1]. The four independent directors (Mihir Shah, Suresh Bhagavatula, Kurian Chandy and Prachi Jain) sat on all committees through FY26. No independent-director resignation appears in the FY23 to FY26 reports, and the statutory auditor, Gupta Raj and Co, is unchanged [1]. The FY26 secretarial audit lists minor lapses: results advertisements published 7.5 hours and more than two days late, and defective charge-modification filings [1]. The related-party schedule deserves attention. Click Retail Pvt Ltd, on whose board whole-time director Vijay Advani sits, is listed in the annual report among entities influenced by key management. It bought ₹26.78 Cr in FY26 and carried a ₹47.74 Cr outstanding balance at year-end, equal to 8.4% of consolidated trade receivables. The schedule does not say whether that balance is trade or advance, and it exceeds the ₹32.45 Cr of related-party trade receivables the notes report [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: PAT rose in every year, while operating cash flow was negative in seven of eight years (FY25 the only exception) before the H1 FY27 swing. [2][12]

web_blocks.text: Four lessons sit inside the table. The one positive year (FY25) is the year the enterprise trade shrank, so growth and cash have been rivals. The cash drains followed strategic expansions. The FY22 to FY24 run of −₹19 Cr to −₹28 Cr came with the Honeywell launches and the enterprise surge. The −₹272 Cr of FY26 came with the new Make-in-India categories. Cash-cycle days nearly doubled from 42 to 75 in FY26 because debtor days jumped from 49 to 76 [12]. Management's 'net working capital days' print the same 42 and 75 at March 2025 and March 2026, so the two measures agree at year-ends. Screener's separate 'working-capital days' line (50 and 47) uses a different formula and is not used in this report [2][12]. Operating margin barely moved for seven years, from 2.8% in FY19 to 3.4% in FY26. The profit growth therefore came almost entirely from scale and from the Honeywell mix, not from better economics in the distribution book [12].

web_blocks.caption: Four operating regimes (₹ Cr; operating margin excludes other income)
rows: Multi-brand distribution funded by IPO cash; Honeywell at ₹25 Cr [2][12]
Low-margin enterprise trade plus Honeywell launches; stock and receivables built [8][12]
Enterprise trade capped; Honeywell and marketing spend scale; first positive cash year [6][12]
India-billed surge, then a liability-funded cash swing [1][10]
web_blocks.takeaway: Profit compounded in all four regimes; cash turned positive only in the last, and only because of a swing in what the company owes. [1][10][12]

web_blocks.text: Regime D deserves a careful reading. In H1 FY27 operating cash flow was +₹351.24 Cr against −₹91.65 Cr a year earlier [10]. Profit before working-capital changes was about ₹63 Cr. Trade payables rose ₹281.9 Cr and other current liabilities rose ₹192.8 Cr. Vendor advances and other assets absorbed ₹116.4 Cr, and receivables still grew ₹51.6 Cr [10]. At 30 September 2026 trade payables stood at ₹467.01 Cr against ₹185.11 Cr at March, and borrowings had fallen to about ₹194 Cr from ₹324 Cr [12]. The turnaround is therefore a liability-side event, financed by suppliers and by advances from counterparties, not a collections event. Management itself says the 45-day working-capital figure will drift back to 52 to 55 days [4].

web_blocks.title: What the FY25 stall and the FY26 jump actually were

web_blocks.text: FY25 looked like a stall and was one. Revenue from operations moved from ₹1,713 Cr [8] to ₹1,774 Cr [3] and total income grew 3.5% [2]. Management's explanation on 16 May 2025 was specific: 'the distribution business has been very flat this year'. Electronics prices erode 15 to 20% a year, so volumes must grow 30 to 35% to show 15% revenue growth, and 'we did not add any new major brands' [6]. The enterprise trade lost a sale of more than ₹200 Cr in Q1 and its gross margin slid from 2.61% to 2.09% [6]. The audited notes agree. Enterprise revenue was ₹1,205.95 Cr against ₹1,211.88 Cr, and FMCT fell from ₹243.80 Cr to ₹182.04 Cr. FMSG, the home of Honeywell, rose from ₹256.56 Cr to ₹385.36 Cr (AR FY25). Geography says the same from another side: revenue billed outside India fell 12.6% to ₹1,096.07 Cr while India-billed revenue rose 47.7% to ₹678.41 Cr (AR FY25). Profit still grew 10% because a brand business with a blended gross margin of 35 to 36% (Q2 FY25 call) gained share while a trade earning about 2% shrank.

The FY26 jump is a different animal. Revenue from operations on the deck basis rose ₹925 Cr (52%) to ₹2,699.77 Cr. That basis excludes ₹4.84 Cr of export entitlements, and the audited statement shows ₹2,704.62 Cr with them. Of the rise, ₹815 Cr (88%) came from Market Entry and ₹110 Cr from Brand [3][1]. All of it was billed in India. India-billed revenue went from ₹678.41 Cr to ₹1,797.13 Cr (+165%) while revenue billed outside India fell 17.6% to ₹902.64 Cr [1]. Q4 FY26 made it vivid. Market Entry revenue doubled from ₹321.13 Cr to ₹663.43 Cr, while Brand fell 6.5% from ₹81.86 Cr to ₹76.58 Cr. That happened as the Middle East war lifted container freight from $1,500–1,700 to $7,500–8,000 [3][5]. Management's explanation is thematic rather than numerical. The last two quarters were spent 'focusing on Make in India companies', mainly surveillance and AI, on new categories such as servers, data-centre products and memory, and on extended credit to new customers. It also cites 30 to 40% cost inflation in memory, storage and CPUs that lifts invoice values [5]. It has never published a vendor-level bridge. Our judgement is that it is more likely than not that most of the extra ₹1,119 Cr of India billing came from new Make-in-India, server, memory and government-linked lines plus price inflation, not from organic growth in the older consumer brands. Those are the categories added in the same year and Honeywell was falling in the quarter that doubled.

The cost was cash. Receivables rose from ₹237.77 Cr to ₹565.11 Cr, from 13.4% to about 21% of turnover. Total borrowings rose from ₹71.80 Cr to ₹324.26 Cr, of which ₹171.19 Cr was TReDS supplier finance used to pay small MSME vendors within 45 days [5][3]. Operating cash flow was −₹271.88 Cr in the audited cash-flow statement [1]. The Q2 FY27 deck prints FY26 operating cash flow as ₹271.88 Cr on one page and ₹273.10 Cr on another. The audited statement says ₹271.88 Cr, so that is the figure used throughout [1][2]. Crisil reaffirmed its BBB+/Stable rating on 6 August 2026. It attributes the working-capital stretch to year-end billing and credit extended to a few customers. It also sets a downward trigger if one customer exceeds 40% of revenue, against about 25% now and 50 to 60% historically [13].

web_blocks.takeaway: Near-term revenue and profit guidance has been met or beaten; multi-year targets for margin, licence scale and cash have been missed by wide margins. [8][3]

web_blocks.text: The ledger gives a clear reading. On revenue and on guidance given within twelve months, this management is credible: FY25 landed inside its range and FY26 profit beat the number it floated in November 2025. On the licence business it is mixed: ₹500 Cr was promised for FY26 and ₹369.61 Cr delivered, with one base year restated to flatter growth. On cash and margin it has been consistently too optimistic. The 5% EBITDA promised by FY25 became 4.04%, a 4.5–5% PAT margin by FY26 became 2.59%, and operating cash flow was positive in one year out of eight. Management now asks investors to accept ₹6,000 Cr of revenue by FY29 with a 40% Brand share [2]. That needs Brand to grow from ₹380.86 Cr to about ₹2,400 Cr, roughly 85% a year for three years against 41% in FY26 and 43% in H1 FY27 [3][2]. We would treat the revenue target as plausible, since the required 30% compound rate is below the 33% achieved since FY19 [2]. The Brand mix we treat as unlikely, roughly one chance in four, because it requires an acquisition or a breakout in WOZOYO or surveillance that has not yet appeared in reported numbers. The next test arrives in March 2027, the date management gave in May 2026 for the Honeywell licence renewal. Earlier statements said December 2025 and end 2027, and no filing reports a renewal event since. Management says it is 'very sure' of renewal [5][6][7].

book_paragraphs: Let me start where the company starts, in 1992, because I want you to feel how small the beginning was. Ketan Patel runs a proprietary trading concern called Creative Computers with, according to the prospectus, ten employees. He sells printers and monitors made by other people. Picture the work in physical terms: a truck of boxes arrives, the boxes are counted into a godown, dealers phone in orders, and the profit is the few percentage points between what he paid the vendor and what the dealer pays him. Everything depends on how quickly the boxes leave and the cheques come back. By the time the company filed its prospectus for the 2017 IPO, that same logic had grown to about 20 branches, roughly 6,000 dealers and ₹198.79 Cr of annual sales. Keep that picture in your head, because the rest of this story is one man's attempt to escape the arithmetic of the thin spread without ever quite leaving the warehouse.

In April 2017 the company listed on the NSE's SME platform, selling 18,00,000 new shares at ₹75 to raise ₹13.50 Cr. That money went into working capital, as the prospectus said it would. The more important event came a year earlier, in the Honeywell licence. Here is what the licence really is. Honeywell does not ship Creative anything. Creative designs a surge protector or an air purifier, finds a factory in China, Taiwan or India, gets Honeywell's auditors to approve the factory and the packaging, and sells it under the Honeywell name. In return it pays Honeywell the greater of a minimum guarantee or a percentage of sales. In Ketan Patel's own words on the August 2023 call: 'we ourself design products, we get it manufactured, the specification is done by us.' That is a brand business with a distributor's logistics, and it lives in a Hong Kong company, Secure Connection, that pays no tax on export profit and in which Creative owns 77.50%.

Now follow the money, because a business that must buy stock before it sells it is always asking someone for capital. Creative has raised it on a ladder of rising prices: ₹75 in the 2017 IPO, ₹110 in 2021, ₹450 in 2023, ₹785 for a share swap in 2024, and ₹1,133.33 for a swap proposed this month to buy Zicom SaaS. Each rung diluted earlier holders, but notice how gentle the dilution has been. Shares went from 1,16,00,000 in April 2021 to 1,50,16,675 today, an increase of 29.5%, while earnings per share rose roughly threefold, from ₹13.32 in FY22 to ₹41.04 in FY26. The cash equity raised after the IPO is about ₹91 Cr. Put that number beside another: about ₹318 Cr of operating cash consumed across FY22 to FY26. Shareholders paid for under a third of the burn. Banks and suppliers paid the rest.

Why does a profitable company burn cash? Mostly because of a product line called enterprise business. Ketan Patel described it in May 2022: 'Enterprise business is an opportunity business and whenever we have free cash flow, we usually use it into that business.' It is back-to-back trading with large corporates at a gross margin of roughly two percent, and in FY22 it grew to ₹542 Cr, more than half of group revenue. That same month the CFO told analysts: 'by September we should be to show a positive cash flow for sure.' It did not happen. Operating cash flow was −₹19 Cr in FY22 and −₹21 Cr in FY23. A year later, in May 2023, he said: 'we will have a positive cash flow this time for sure.' FY24 came in at −₹28 Cr. I am not scoring points. I am telling you that when a team promises the same result in the same words two years running and misses both times, you should discount the third promise.

In March 2024 the company did something I rarely see in promoter-run businesses: it sold a pet project. CKart, a B2B ordering platform launched with some fanfare, went for ₹10 Cr and left a ₹9.9 Cr gain. Ketan Patel's explanation was blunt: 'our balance sheet can't afford burning money for a business.' That is real discipline. It also flattered FY24. The CFO told analysts to strip ₹7.71 Cr out of EBITDA and profit, which takes FY24 PAT from ₹48.25 Cr to about ₹40.5 Cr and turns the reported 10% profit growth of FY25 into something nearer 31% underlying. In the same quarter the enterprise trade shrank by about ₹90 Cr year on year because it could not clear the company's 20% return-on-capital hurdle. Notice the rule: enterprise business is switched on when cash is spare and off when it is not. It behaves like a cash-management tool disguised as a revenue line.

FY25 is the year to study if you want to understand the engine. Revenue grew 3.5%. Ketan Patel said it plainly on the 16 May 2025 call: 'the distribution business has been very flat this year.' Electronics prices erode 15 to 20% a year, the company had lost an enterprise sale of more than ₹200 Cr in the first quarter, and 'we did not add any new major brands.' While the top line stood still, two things went right. Honeywell grew 50% to ₹255.17 Cr, and operating cash flow turned positive for the first time in the data set, at +₹21.86 Cr. The CFO said he was pleased that 'our operating cash flow has turned positive after a long time.' The lesson is uncomfortable. The only year the company generated cash was the year the enterprise trade shrank. Growth and cash have been rivals, not partners.

Then came FY26, and the engine roared. Revenue from operations rose ₹925 Cr, about 88% of it from Market Entry, and all of it billed inside India: Indian billing went from ₹678 Cr to ₹1,797 Cr while billing outside India fell. In the fourth quarter alone Market Entry revenue doubled while Honeywell, hit by Red Sea freight that went from $1,500–1,700 to $7,500–8,000 a container, slipped. The new money came from new vendors, small Indian surveillance and AI makers. Ketan Patel explained the attraction: 'the vendors whom we are dealing with, their size is much smaller and that's why you get a higher percentage margin.' Small vendors have little credit to give, so Creative pays early and extends credit to government-linked buyers. Receivables rose from ₹237.77 Cr to ₹565.11 Cr and operating cash flow was −₹271.88 Cr. Asked about it, Ketan Patel said: 'I will also agree that we have to do a better job in the debtor receivable days.'

The latest half-year flips the story. Operating cash flow was +₹351.24 Cr and management reports net working capital of 45 days, down from 75. Before you applaud, open the cash-flow statement the way I would. Profit before working capital was about ₹63 Cr. Trade payables rose ₹281.9 Cr and other liabilities, which include advances from counterparties, rose ₹192.8 Cr. Vendor advances and other assets absorbed ₹116.4 Cr, and receivables still grew ₹51.6 Cr. So the turnaround was financed by suppliers and customers, not by faster collection. The CFO was candid about the 45-day figure: 'we don't feel that, that is going to be sustainable in the long run', and he guided to 52 to 55 days. A cycle like this can unwind as quickly as it formed, so the next two balance sheets matter more than the last cash-flow statement.

Walk the corridor of governance with me. The CFO who presented every set of numbers from May 2022 to November 2025 resigned on 14 April 2026. His successor, hired as Vice President–Finance on 4 December 2025, took over on 14 May 2026, the day before the FY26 call. The handover looks planned. The co-founder Purvi Patel stepped off the board in August 2025 'to pursue philanthropic and social work independently' and was back inside the company 15 days later as head of strategy on the same pay. The four independent directors have not changed, and the auditor has not changed. The related-party schedule, on the other hand, is busy: Secure Connection supplied ₹155.39 Cr of goods in FY26, shareholders were asked to approve up to ₹750 Cr for FY27, and a director-linked retailer, Click Retail, carried a ₹47.74 Cr outstanding balance at year-end that the notes do not fully explain. None of this is improper on its face. It simply means the quality of the numbers rests on trusting a small circle.

Put the promises on one page and a pattern appears. On revenue, management has met or beaten itself: FY26 revenue from operations of ₹2,699.77 Cr (₹2,704.62 Cr in the audited statement, which adds ₹4.84 Cr of export entitlements) against the ₹2,100–2,200 Cr it called for three years earlier, FY25 inside the guided ₹1,600–1,900 Cr range, and FY26 profit of ₹70.29 Cr against ₹60 Cr 'or slightly better'. On the licence business the record is mixed. In May 2023 the CFO said 'we will at least be INR500 crores in Honeywell or any other brand' by FY26; the delivered figure was ₹369.61 Cr. In May 2024 the FY23 base was described as 'Rs. 80 crores odd' so that growth could be called more than 100%, when the company's own May 2023 figure was ₹108 Cr and growth was 57%. On cash and margins the record is poor: 5% EBITDA by FY25 became 4.04%, a 4.5–5% PAT margin by FY26 became 2.59%, and operating cash flow was positive in one year out of eight.

One date sits over everything: March 2027, when the Honeywell licence comes up for renewal. Ketan Patel says: 'we are very sure that the Honeywell license will get renewed after March '27', and he points out that Honeywell itself is splitting into separate companies. Notice, though, that the licence term has been described four different ways in the filings and calls: 31 December 2020 in the prospectus, December 2025 in May 2025, the end of 2027 in November 2025, and March 2027 in May 2026. The December 2025 date has also passed without any disclosed renewal event, and by May 2026 the chairman was again describing March 2027 as the next renewal. I do not read that as a warning, only as a reason to ask for the paperwork. Management agreed in November 2025 that the brand business supplies roughly half the group's EBITDA on about 14% of revenue. The licence is therefore the one asset whose loss or repricing the business could not absorb, and its renewal terms are the first thing I would want to see.

So what does the history tell you? Three things. First, this is a company that spots categories early and moves before the numbers justify it: air purifiers, quick commerce, Make-in-India surveillance. Second, it grows by adding capital-hungry business lines and then discovers the working-capital bill, usually a year after the revenue. Every one of the four regimes shows profit rising while cash lagged. Third, its management gives dependable one-year guidance and undependable three-year aspirations. It now asks you to accept ₹6,000 Cr of revenue by FY29 with a 40% Brand share, which means Brand growing from ₹381 Cr to ₹2,400 Cr, roughly 85% a year for three years. Ketan Patel himself cautions: 'you should not be overconfident', because 'something keeps happening, right?' I would treat the revenue target as plausible and the brand mix as unlikely, about one chance in four. Judge the next 12 months by cash conversion first and by headline growth second.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: I keep returning to the first number in this chapter: cumulative reported profit of ₹241 Cr set against cumulative operating cash of about −₹328 Cr across FY19 to FY26. The business has been funded by other people's patience: banks, MSME suppliers through TReDS, and lately supplier credit. That is not a flaw while the patience is renewable. It is a fatal flaw the day it is not. Your task is to work out which kind of patience this is, and the only honest way is to watch cash, not profit, over several balance sheets.

book_callouts.title: THE PROMISE-VERSUS-CASH TEST
book_callouts.text: Whenever management states a multi-year aspiration for margin or growth, put two numbers beside it: operating cash flow in the same year and the change in receivable plus inventory days. Credibility is earned where the aspiration and the cash agree. Here, revenue guidance passes the test and margin and cash guidance have failed it, so weight the first accordingly.
